claims.text: The Machine Payments Protocol (MPP) is an open protocol for machine-to-machine payments that lets a client pay inside an HTTP exchange using the 402 Payment Required status code.
MPP is co-authored by Tempo and Stripe; it is not a Stripe-only protocol.
The mpp-specs README names Tempo Labs and Stripe as the organizations that maintain the specification.
The core draft lists five authors: Brendan Ryan, Jake Moxey and Tom Meagher of Tempo Labs, and Jeff Weinstein and Steve Kaliski of Stripe.
The core specification is titled The 'Payment' HTTP Authentication Scheme and defines a Payment scheme used with HTTP 402.
The core is an individual Internet-Draft listed under Individual Submissions on the IETF Datatracker, with no working group, no stream and no intended status; it is not an IETF standard.
The MPP specification is split into a core, intents, payment methods and extensions such as discovery and transports.
MPP specification documents are released under CC0 1.0, and the repository tooling is licensed Apache-2.0 or MIT at the user's option.
The mppx TypeScript SDK repository is licensed MIT.
MPP governance sends the core specification through the IETF while each payment method is defined and maintained by the rail behind it.
MPP has no foundation, charter or steering committee in any of its repositories.
Payment rails can add MPP payment methods without approval, and mppx supports custom payment methods.
New MPP intents start as experimental definitions inside a method spec and move to specs/intents only after two or more methods adopt them.
Stripe announced MPP on 2026-03-18, the same day Tempo announced its mainnet.
Tempo's mainnet post calls Visa a design partner that extended MPP to card payments on its network.
Tempo's mainnet post says Stripe extended MPP to cards, wallets and other methods through its platform, and Lightspark extended it to Bitcoin payments over Lightning.

Tempo's mainnet post names Anthropic, DoorDash, Mastercard, Nubank, OpenAI, Ramp, Revolut, Shopify, Standard Chartered and Visa as partners for stablecoin use cases on Tempo mainnet, not as MPP design partners.
MPP is not crypto-only: its methods include Stripe Shared Payment Tokens, a Visa-authored card method and Lightning.
In AP2 documents the abbreviation MPP means Merchant Payment Processor, a role unrelated to the Machine Payments Protocol.
draft-ryan-httpauth-payment-00 was posted to the IETF Datatracker on 2026-02-16 (UTC).
draft-ryan-httpauth-payment-01 was posted on 2026-03-18 (UTC).
The Datatracker recorded draft-ryan-httpauth-payment as expired on 2026-09-18.
draft-httpauth-payment-00 was published on 2026-06-19, while draft-ryan-httpauth-payment-01 was still active.
draft-httpauth-payment-01 was published on 2026-09-09 and expires on 2027-03-13.
The 2026-09-09 change was the -01 revision of draft-httpauth-payment, not the rename; the new draft name first appeared on 2026-06-19.
The IETF Datatracker records no replaces relation between draft-ryan-httpauth-payment and draft-httpauth-payment.
The MPP intent, method, discovery and MCP transport drafts are not on the IETF Datatracker; only the core draft is.
The tempoxyz/mpp-specs repository was created on 2026-01-05 and its first commit became public on 2026-03-18.
The MPP core carries no version on the wire; an incompatible change would need a new scheme name such as Payment2.
MPP payment methods may add a version field in methodDetails, and its absence means version 1.
The Solana charge method was merged into mpp-specs on 2026-03-24.
The Stellar charge method was merged on 2026-03-29.
The Accept-Payment negotiation header was merged into the core spec on 2026-04-13.
The unified EVM charge method was merged on 2026-04-17.
The Hedera charge method was merged on 2026-05-14 and the Hedera session method on 2026-08-07.
Circle's usdc charge method was merged on 2026-06-16.
The NEAR Intents charge method was first merged on 2026-06-21.
The XRPL charge and session methods were merged on 2026-09-08.
The subscription intent spec, with Stripe and Tempo subscription methods, was merged on 2026-07-29.
The MPP blog announced subscriptions on 2026-05-12, the same day mppx 0.6.20 added Tempo subscriptions.
Tempo session v2 was announced on the MPP blog on 2026-06-17 and its spec text was merged on 2026-06-25.
The header parameter and the Payment-Authorization field were merged into the core spec on 2026-08-25.
mppx 0.6.29, published 2026-06-02, added EVM charge support with x402 exact compatibility; the MPP blog post on EVM and x402 support is dated 2026-06-08.
TAP and Web Bot Auth attestation was merged into mppx on 2026-08-04, first shipped on npm in 0.8.17 on 2026-08-10, and announced on the MPP blog on 2026-08-12.
mppx 0.9.0, published 2026-08-27, added dual MPP and x402 wrappers for Express, Hono, Next.js and MCP and a requiresAuth option that uses Payment-Authorization.
The latest mppx release is 0.13.4, published 2026-10-08.
The mppx npm package was created on 2026-02-12.
A pull request to add a generic session intent (mpp-specs PR #280) was closed without merging on 2026-09-28.
As of 2026-10-11 specs/intents in mpp-specs contains only the charge and subscription intents; session is defined inside individual method specs.
A client MUST verify the requested amount, recipient, currency and validity window before authorizing payment and MUST NOT rely on the description parameter.
MPP servers MUST NOT perform side effects for requests that have not been paid.
MPP servers MUST NOT require user accounts for payment.
In the card method a Client Enabler provisions an encrypted network token and cryptogram, and a Server Enabler decrypts it and requests authorization from the card network.
The stripe method identifies the merchant by a Stripe Business Network Profile ID in methodDetails.networkId, and both client and server need Stripe accounts.
A Payment challenge requires the parameters id, realm, method, intent and request.
Optional challenge parameters are digest, expires, description, header and opaque.
The request parameter is base64url-encoded JSON without padding, serialized with the JSON Canonicalization Scheme of RFC 8785.
Servers MUST bind the challenge id to realm, method, intent and request, and to expires, digest, opaque and header when present; description is excluded.
The recommended stateless binding computes the challenge id as base64url HMAC-SHA256 over realm, method, intent, request, expires, digest, an optional header slot and opaque, joined by pipes.
The only allowed value of the header parameter is Payment-Authorization, and it tells the client to send the credential in that field instead of Authorization.
Payment-Authorization lets a client keep an ordinary bearer token in Authorization while sending the Payment credential separately.
A Payment credential is base64url JSON with a required challenge echo, an optional source payer identifier (DID format recommended) and a required method-specific payload.
The Payment-Receipt header carries base64url JSON with status, method, timestamp and reference, and status is always success.
Servers MUST NOT send Payment-Receipt on error responses.
Payment method identifiers are lowercase ASCII letters only.
Accept-Payment lists method and intent pairs with optional q weights and wildcards, for example tempo/charge or */session, and q=0 means do not use.
The WWW-Authenticate challenge stays authoritative even when the client sends Accept-Payment.
MPP error bodies use RFC 9457 problem details with type URIs under https://paymentauth.org/problems/.

The core problem types are payment-required, payment-insufficient, payment-expired, verification-failed, method-unsupported, malformed-credential, invalid-challenge, bad-request, invalid-payload, internal-payment-error and payment-action-required.
The charge intent request requires amount in base units and currency, with optional recipient, description, externalId and methodDetails.
Challenge expiry travels only as the expires auth-param and must not be duplicated inside the request object.
The subscription intent request requires amount, currency, periodUnit (day, week or month) and periodCount, with optional subscriptionExpires.
On subscription activation the server MUST return a subscriptionId in the Payment-Receipt.
The Tempo session request carries amount as a price per unit, plus currency, recipient, optional unitType and suggestedDeposit, and a required methodDetails.escrowContract.
The Tempo session payload action is one of open, topUp, voucher or close.
A Tempo session voucher carries channelId, cumulativeAmount and an EIP-712 signature, and amounts are cumulative totals, not deltas.
The stripe charge method's request requires methodDetails.networkId and methodDetails.paymentMethodTypes, and its payload carries an spt field holding a Shared Payment Token id starting with spt_.
The card method's request requires methodDetails.acceptedNetworks and merchantName, plus an RSA encryption key as encryptionJwk or as jwksUri with kid.

The card credential payload carries encryptedPayload (a JWE), network, panLastFour, panExpirationMonth, panExpirationYear and, when available, billingAddress, cardholderFullName and paymentAccountReference.
The Tempo charge method supports methodDetails chainId, feePayer, memo, splits and supportedModes, and payload types transaction, hash and proof.
The Tempo subscription method uses an access key authorization with keyType p256, secp256k1 or webAuthn, and allows only day or week billing periods.
The mpp-specs repository defines eleven payment method identifiers: tempo, stripe, card, lightning, evm, solana, stellar, hedera, usdc, nearintents and xrpl.
mpp.dev also documents monad and redotpay payment methods that have no spec file in mpp-specs.
The card method spec is authored by Jacob Brans of Visa.
The lightning method (BOLT11 invoices) is authored by Lightspark and defines charge and session intents.
The usdc method spec is authored by Circle Internet Group.
The evm charge spec lists authors from Coinbase, MegaETH Labs and Monad Foundation, and the evm session spec lists authors from OKG.
Session intents are defined for the tempo, evm, solana, hedera, lightning and xrpl methods.
The core draft asks IANA to register Accept-Payment, Payment-Authorization and Payment-Receipt as permanent header fields and to create HTTP Payment Methods and HTTP Payment Intents registries.
As of 2026-10-11 IANA lists neither the Payment authentication scheme nor the Accept-Payment, Payment-Authorization or Payment-Receipt fields.

In the basic flow the server answers an unpaid request with 402 and WWW-Authenticate: Payment, the client pays and retries with Authorization: Payment, and the server returns 200 with Payment-Receipt.
A malformed credential, an unknown or used challenge, an expired challenge or a failed proof each get a 402 with a fresh challenge and a matching problem type.
A 403 response means the payment was valid but policy denies access, and it carries no new challenge.
When a resource needs both authentication and payment, servers SHOULD check authentication first and return 401 before issuing a 402 Payment challenge.
Servers SHOULD reject a request that carries more than one Payment credential with 400.
The charge intent forbids partial delivery, such as streamed tokens or tool calls, before payment verification succeeds.
In the stripe charge flow the server creates a PaymentIntent with confirm true and the SPT as shared_payment_granted_token, and returns a receipt only when the PaymentIntent status is succeeded.
The stripe charge spec recommends an idempotency key built from the challenge id and the SPT when creating the PaymentIntent.
Stripe Connect parameters such as application_fee_amount and transfer_data come from server configuration and MUST NOT appear in the MPP challenge.
In a Tempo session the client deposits into an escrow, signs rising vouchers per unit consumed, and the server settles on-chain when it chooses.
Tempo session vouchers are sent to the same resource URI, and HEAD requests may carry voucher-only updates.
On a cooperative close in session v2 the server captures max(spent, settled on-chain) and refunds the rest of the deposit to the payer.
A forced close starts when the client calls requestClose, waits a grace period of at least 15 minutes during which the server can still settle, and ends when the client calls withdraw.
The Tempo session spec advises clients to wait at least 16 minutes after requestClose before calling withdraw.
Subscription servers may collect at most one renewal per billing period, and missed periods do not add up to extra charging authority.
Possession of a subscriptionId alone does not authorize use of a subscription.
Tempo payment channels have no expiry and remain open until explicitly closed, and vouchers have no validUntil field.
Tempo session v1 uses the TempoStreamChannel escrow contract, and v2 uses a TIP-20 channel reserve precompile selected by methodDetails.sessionProtocol.
Tempo session vouchers use the EIP-712 domain name Tempo Stream Channel in v1 and TIP20 Channel Reserve in v2.
In the MCP transport a paid method returns JSON-RPC error -32042 Payment Required with challenges in error.data.
In the MCP transport the credential travels in _meta under org.paymentauth/credential and the receipt under org.paymentauth/receipt.
In the MCP transport a failed payment verification returns JSON-RPC error -32043 with a fresh challenge.
MCP servers SHOULD advertise payment support under capabilities.experimental.payment.methods in InitializeResult.
For SSE streams a session receipt is sent in the initial headers and again as a final payment-receipt event.
MPP discovery is optional and uses an OpenAPI document at /openapi.json with x-service-info and per-operation x-payment-info extensions.
The discovery draft is co-authored by Tempo Labs and Merit Systems.
Discovery metadata is advisory and the 402 challenge stays authoritative.
MPP requires TLS 1.2 or later for all Payment flows and recommends TLS 1.3.
The digest challenge parameter uses RFC 9530 to bind a payment to the request body.
Tempo session vouchers are signed with ECDSA over secp256k1 as EIP-712 typed data.
The card method encrypts the network token and cryptogram as a JWE for the server's RSA key, and neither client nor server may parse it.
Payment credentials are bearer tokens that servers and intermediaries MUST NOT log or include in errors or analytics.
Payment methods MUST provide single-use proofs, and each challenge id may be used only once.
Servers MUST send Cache-Control: no-store on 402 responses and Cache-Control: private on responses with Payment-Receipt.
Because RFC 9111 shared-cache protection applies to Authorization but not to Payment-Authorization, responses to requests using Payment-Authorization must be private or no-store.
A Tempo session caps the payer's exposure at the channel deposit, since vouchers cannot exceed the deposit.
CVE-2026-34209 (GHSA-mv9j-8jvg-j8mr) is a high-severity mppx bug before 0.4.11 where a session close voucher equal to the settled amount was accepted, closing or griefing a channel for free.
CVE-2026-34210 (GHSA-8mhj-rffc-rcvw) is a medium-severity mppx bug before 0.4.11 where stripe/charge ignored Stripe's Idempotent-Replayed header, so one SPT credential could be replayed.
The GitHub advisories for CVE-2026-34209 and CVE-2026-34210 and the fix release mppx 0.4.11 are dated 2026-03-26, and NVD published both CVEs on 2026-03-31.

GHSA-fxc9-7j2w-vx54 is a critical advisory for the Rust crate mpp before 0.8.0 covering free and replayed charges, session griefing, fee-payer manipulation and replayed stripe charges; it has no CVE id.
GHSA-8x4m-qw58-3pcx is a critical advisory for mppx before 0.4.8 covering several tempo/charge and tempo/session payment bypasses; it has no CVE id.
CVE-2026-63627 and CVE-2026-63628 are medium-severity mppx advisories from 2026-07-01 in which the server fee payer could be drained through calldata padding or access lists, fixed in 0.8.2.
arXiv:2609.00060 builds Tamarin models of x402, MPP, ACP and AP2 and reports 40 previously undocumented formal-consistency findings across them.
MPP has no native agent identity; mppx adds optional RFC 9421 request attestation for Web Bot Auth and Visa TAP.
Spending limits in MPP come from the rail: a session deposit, SPT usage limits, or Tempo access key limits.
Disputes in MPP depend on the payment method: card routes keep chargebacks while Stripe stablecoin payments have no disputes.
MPP defines no protocol-level kill switch or revocation message; subscriptions are cancelled through method-specific means.
Tempo settlement is public on-chain, and MPPscan by Merit Systems indexes MPP servers, agents, transactions and volume.
The mpp.dev payments directory is published as JSON at https://mpp.dev/api/services.
The MPP specs define no .well-known path; discovery uses /openapi.json.
Stripe says MPP payments appear in the Stripe API and Dashboard and settle to the merchant's existing balance and payout schedule.
The stripe method keeps raw card data away from client and server, which the spec says reduces PCI DSS scope.
TIP-20 tokens can reference TIP-403 policy registry allow and block lists.
Official MPP SDKs exist for TypeScript (mppx), Python (pympp), Rust (mpp), Go (mpp-go) and Ruby (mpp-rb).
The Ruby SDK mpp-rb is hosted in the stripe/mpp-rb repository.
Visa publishes the mpp-card npm package (0.1.8) that implements the card method with the charge intent.
The mpp.dev payments directory listed 129 services on 2026-10-11, of which 126 accept tempo, 10 stripe and 1 evm.
At launch Tempo said the payments directory had more than 100 services, including Alchemy, Dune Analytics, Merit Systems and Parallel Web Systems.
Stripe's launch post names Browserbase, PostalForm, Prospect Butcher Co. and Stripe Climate as MPP users and quotes Parallel Web Systems.
At Sessions on 2026-04-29 Stripe said businesses can accept MPP payments in stablecoins and in cards, Klarna and Affirm through Shared Payment Tokens on the Payment Intents API.
At Sessions on 2026-04-29 Stripe announced streaming payments by combining Metronome and Tempo; the recap does not say these run over MPP.
Cloudflare's Agents docs describe MPP, use mppx in their guides, and say MPP is backwards compatible with x402.
Stripe's MPP integration creates crypto deposit addresses on Tempo and off-ramps stablecoin payments into the Stripe balance.
Stripe labels its MPP documentation Frontier and uses the preview API version 2026-07-29.preview.
Tempo mainnet has chain ID 4217 and the Moderato testnet has chain ID 42431.
Tempo has no native token and charges transaction fees in USD-denominated TIP-20 stablecoins through a Fee AMM.
Tempo uses Simplex BFT consensus with deterministic finality and produces blocks about every 600 ms.
Tempo's validator set is permissioned.
TIP-20 tokens always use 6 decimals.
Tempo charge defaults chainId to 42431 and Tempo session defaults to 4217, while the Tempo subscription spec mislabels 42431 as Tempo mainnet.
For a 50,000-gas transfer Tempo's base fee is capped at about $0.0006 with a quiet-period floor near $0.00003.
Stripe's MPP minimum is 0.50 USD for card payments through Shared Payment Tokens and 0.01 USDC for stablecoin payments.
With hostedFeePayer true, Stripe pays customers' Tempo network fees; it needs mppx 0.9.2 or later, live mode and a Tempo deposit address on the same account, and does not work with Connect.
When methodDetails.feePayer is true the server co-signs the Tempo transaction and pays its fees, and the server always pays fees for settle and close.
A 1.5 percent fee for Stripe stablecoin payments was reported in December 2025; whether it applies to MPP stablecoin charges is not stated by Stripe.
Whether Stripe charges a percentage fee on MPP stablecoin payments received through deposit addresses is unverified.
Stripe stablecoin payments have a 10,000 USD per-transaction customer limit, no disputes, and refunds in stablecoin to the original wallet.
No public fee schedule for Stripe Shared Payment Tokens was found.
Tempo session v2 cut gas for opening a channel with an existing reserve balance by 72.1 percent but raised gas for settling to a new payee balance by 79.4 percent.
The MPP spec defines no protocol fee; costs come from the payment rail.
MPPscan reported 4,072,426 MPP transactions, 435,476 USD of volume, 224,244 unique senders and 6,101 unique recipients all time as of 2026-10-11.
MPPscan reported 998,771 transactions and 8,774 USD of volume in the 30 days to 2026-10-11, under one cent per transaction on average.
MPPscan's homepage showed 126,902 transactions, 1,484 USD, 3,711 senders and 167 recipients for the 7 days to 2026-10-11.
The Merit Systems glossary page dated June 24, 2026 shows live hourly MPPscan figures, so its 4.1M transactions and 435.4K USD are 2026-10-11 values, not June values.
Visa and Artemis measured about 25,000 USD across about 115,000 MPP transfers up to 2026-04-21.
The tempoxyz/mpp-specs repository had 95 GitHub stars and wevm/mppx had 186 on 2026-10-11.
MPP's comparison page maps the x402 PAYMENT-REQUIRED header to WWW-Authenticate: Payment, PAYMENT-SIGNATURE to Authorization: Payment and PAYMENT-RESPONSE to Payment-Receipt.
MPP's documentation says the x402 exact scheme maps onto the MPP charge intent, and x402 upto and EVM batch-settlement are its usage-based counterparts to the MPP session intent.
With mppx a server can emit both MPP and x402 challenges on one route, accept either credential, and return the matching receipt header.
The mppx client prefers Payment-auth challenges over x402 challenges when both are offered.
The MPP discovery draft cites x402scan's OpenAPI-first discovery and its /.well-known/x402 fallback as prior art.
The card method spec says a client may add Visa Trusted Agent Protocol signature headers, and this wording has been in the spec since its public release on 2026-03-18.
Visa's 2026-03-18 announcement says its card spec and SDK for MPP are built on Visa Intelligent Commerce and the Trusted Agent Protocol.
The mpp-card 0.1.8 package contains Client Enabler adapters but no Trusted Agent Protocol signing code.
The card method spec points Client Enablers to network services such as Visa Intelligent Commerce for agent-specific tokens.
The stripe MPP method carries Stripe Shared Payment Tokens, the same token family Stripe uses for agentic checkout alongside ACP.
The cloned UCP, ACP, AP2, ERC-8004 and Mastercard toolkit repositories contain no reference to the Machine Payments Protocol.
The MPP discovery draft compares itself with ERC-8004 and says it is off-chain but compatible with future on-chain anchoring.
Tempo and Stripe are in the initial partner group of Mastercard Agent Pay for Machines announced on 2026-06-10.
No Tempo or Mastercard page confirming that Agent Pay for Machines is MPP-compatible could be found, so that claim is unverified.
The Visa card method accepts mastercard as a network value, but no Mastercard-authored MPP method spec exists.
Stripe both co-authors MPP and sits on the x402 Foundation Technical Steering Committee.
All five core authors work at Tempo Labs or Stripe, and there is no neutral working group or steering body.
mpp.dev says the core is submitted to the IETF standards track, but the Datatracker lists it as an individual submission with no stream or intended status.
The MPP blog of 2026-06-17 says sessions are now a formal MPP intent, but the linked pull request was closed unmerged and session is still defined per method.
Open MPP payment channels and unsettled vouchers persist until closed, and the spec only advises servers to close channels idle for about 30 days or more.
The MPP vs x402 page is written by MPP's authors and recommends MPP by default.
Both the TypeScript and Rust MPP SDKs had critical multi-bug advisories within two weeks of launch.
arXiv:2604.15367, SoK: Security of Autonomous LLM Agents in Agentic Commerce (2026-04-15), includes MPP in its protocol set.
PayWord and MicroMint by Rivest and Shamir appeared in Lecture Notes in Computer Science in 1997 with DOI 10.1007/3-540-62494-5_6.
Sprites and State Channels (arXiv:1702.05812, 2017) is a foundation for the payment-channel design MPP sessions use.
In Mastercard's 2026-06-10 Agent Pay for Machines release, Tempo says it is working with Mastercard on Machine Payments Protocol compatibility; Mastercard's own text makes no MPP claim.
No Tempo page listing Agent Pay for Machines as MPP-compatible was found; the compatibility statement exists only as Tempo's quote inside Mastercard's release.
A Tempo session receipt adds challengeId, channelId, acceptedCumulative and spent to the core fields, plus optional units and txHash; its reference is the channelId.
Calling topUp on a Tempo channel with a pending close request cancels that request and emits a CloseRequestCancelled event.
In the Tempo session escrow, open, topUp, requestClose and withdraw are called by the payer, while settle and close are called by the payee.
Subscription servers must collect the renewal for a period before, or atomically with, delivering that period's service.
Expiry, cancellation, a failed renewal or an invalid credential each make a subscription server answer 402 with a fresh challenge.
Stripe's Shared Payment Tokens documentation is labeled Public preview and shows no price schedule as of 2026-10-11.
Over MCP, challenges carry request as a native JSON object instead of base64url, and error.data.httpStatus should be 402.
In the Tempo charge method the client signs a transfer or transferWithMemo transaction whose validBefore is no later than the challenge expires value; with feePayer true the server sponsors the fee.
